paras: The lynching of California Joe, Miguel Barrera and Escolástico Perea took place in Albuquerque, New Mexico Territory, on the night of January 31, 1881, when armed men took the three Mexican prisoners from the county jail and hanged them from its portal. The men had been arrested for the murder of Colonel Charles Potter of the United States Geological Survey, the stepson of a former governor of Rhode Island, and wire dispatches carried the news nationally within two days.

Potter, who had been collecting census statistics, left Albuquerque on October 14, 1880, for the New Placer mining camp and was not heard from again. In late January Sheriff Armijo of Bernalillo County arrested Perea at Isleta, and Perea confessed that he had witnessed the killing without taking part. The sheriff rode with him to the site and returned with Potter's remains, and Barrera and California Joe were arrested at Tejon and Madera. A Dallas Daily Herald dispatch added that another man said to have shared in the murder, Pantaleon Liera, had already been hanged by vigilantes at Bernalillo for horse stealing, and predicted that the three prisoners would follow him "before another day."

According to the Las Vegas Morning Gazette, Sheriff Perfecto Armijo brought Barrera and California Joe to the Albuquerque jail, where Perea was already held, late on Monday, January 31, and left them with five or six guards while he went out of town. Shortly after 8 o'clock a delegation told the parish priest that the three had an hour and a half to live. The priest heard their confessions, and as he left a body of armed men forced their way into the jail and ordered the guards to surrender.

Forty or fifty citizens stood at the entrance, half to two-thirds of them Mexicans, according to the Gazette. The prisoners were dragged to the front of the jail with ropes around their necks, the ropes were thrown over the top of the portal, and the bodies hung there until early morning. Wire dispatches described a band of masked men who spoke not a word and finished in scarcely fifteen minutes, while the German-language Westbote reported that the three bodies were found hanging from a balcony of the jail at sunrise on February 1.

The sheriff was reported to be pursuing a man named Leiber or Leibor, called the principal in Potter's murder. No report of an inquest or of any arrest of the lynchers appears in the coverage. On February 25 a Galveston News dispatch reported that Fanstine Guiterro, implicated in the same murder, had been taken from the jail by vigilantes and hanged where "his accomplices" had been hanged.

The story spread through two wire channels. A Galveston News dispatch from Albuquerque ran on February 2 in the New York Sun and the Lancaster Daily Intelligencer, the latter beneath a long sketch of Potter's family and career. A New Orleans Times special datelined Denison, Texas, ran in the Washington Evening Star, the New-York Tribune, the Portland Daily Press and other papers under heads such as "Three Murderers Lynched," and its dateline led some digests to place the lynching at Denison.

Most of this copy called the dead men "the murderers of Colonel Potter," and weekly summaries reduced the event to a sentence about Mexicans "hanged by citizens." The Dallas Daily Herald wrote that "the souls of three villains had gone to meet him whom they had slain." The Las Vegas Gazette, the only territorial paper in the coverage, headlined its account "STRETCHED," insisted the gathering was "no mob," said the men were dragged out "like dogs, as they were," and concluded that Albuquerque had shown itself a civilized community.

The Gazette, the Chicago Tribune and the Batesville Guard put the lynching on Monday night, January 31, while the Denison wire said Sunday night. The Gazette was the nearest source, and the Dallas dispatch of January 31 still spoke of the lynching as expected, so January 31 is better supported. One digest said five of Potter's murderers had been lynched rather than three, and the victims' names appear in many spellings.

accounts.gist: While a minstrel show played in the courtroom, unknown hands hanged the three; at sunrise Feb. 1 their bodies were seen hanging from a balcony at the front of the county jail.

framing.detail: Las Vegas Gazette headlined 'STRETCHED', said 'It was no mob', called the men 'righteously-condemned' and 'villains', and said Albuquerque had shown it would tolerate no violence.
Dallas Daily Herald closed its dispatch with 'the souls of three villains had gone to meet him whom they had slain'.
The Denison wire ran under heads like 'Three Murderers Lynched' and 'Col. Potter's Murderers Lynched', naming the men as 'the murderers of Colonel Potter'.
Chicago Tribune and weekly digests gave one-sentence notices, 'hanged by citizens' or 'by a party of lynchers'.

conflicts.note: The Las Vegas Gazette is the nearest account and Der Westbote has the bodies found at sunrise Feb. 1; the Dallas Jan. 31 dispatch still predicts the lynching, so Jan. 31 is better supported.
